findings.title: SQL injection via concatenated search term
findings.evidence: The new query is built as 'q = "SELECT * FROM docs WHERE title LIKE '%" + term + "%"'' and executed with no parameter tuple on the next line, so any quote/UNION/OR-1=1 payload in the search term (e.g. a user typing ' OR 1=1 --) becomes executable SQL.
findings.evidence_quote: q = "SELECT * FROM docs WHERE title LIKE '%" + term + "%'"
findings.recommendation: Revert to parameter binding: build the SQL with placeholders and pass the pattern as a bound argument, e.g. 'q = "SELECT * FROM docs WHERE title LIKE ?"' then 'db.execute(q, (f"%{term}%",))'. Never splice caller input into SQL text; if LIKE wildcards must be escaped, escape 'term' (replace % and _ and use ESCAPE) while keeping the value bound.

findings.title: Unescaped term is also treated as LIKE wildcard pattern
findings.evidence: Because the term is interpolated straight into a LIKE pattern string, a term containing '%' or '_' silently changes match semantics (a bare '%' returns every row) instead of being matched literally.
findings.evidence_quote: q = "SELECT * FROM docs WHERE title LIKE '%" + term + "%'"
findings.recommendation: After restoring bound parameters, escape LIKE metacharacters in the term (e.g. term.replace('\\', '\\\\').replace('%', '\\%').replace('_', '\\_')) and add 'ESCAPE \\' to the LIKE clause so user input matches literally.

findings.title: No test covering injection or quoted input in search
findings.evidence: The search path was changed with no test run; nothing exercises a term containing a single quote or SQL fragment, so this regression could ship silently.
findings.recommendation: Add tests asserting that a term such as "a' OR 1=1 --" performs a literal (empty-result) search and raises no SQL error, and that normal terms still match, using an in-memory SQLite database.
